primary_keyword: Cities Within a Drawn Area Finder
title: Cities Within a Drawn Area Finder
description: List the cities and towns inside any polygon you draw with the Cities Within a Drawn Area Finder — OpenStreetMap places, point-in-polygon. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a polygon drawn around the Isle of Wight returns the island's towns — Newport, Ryde, Cowes — and nothing from the mainland: the boundary you drew is the whole rule.
quick_answer: The Cities Within a Drawn Area Finder lists the cities and towns OpenStreetMap records inside a polygon you draw on the map. Click three corners, press the button, and browse places sorted by distance from the shape's centre — the shape-based answer circles cannot give along coasts, valleys and borders.
steps_intro: Circles are lazy shapes. When the real boundary is a coastline or a county line, draw it:

body.t: A sales territory drawn along real boundaries — a river, a ridge, a motorway — contains a specific set of towns. This finder names them, ready for the
Draw the commuter shed you actually mean — not a circle that includes the sea — and get the towns inside it as your search list.
Which communities fall inside a proposed zone, a festival footprint or a consultation area? The polygon decides, and the list is the working document.
Regions are arguments. Drawing one and listing its settlements makes the argument concrete — and shows how a boundary change moves towns in and out.

Trace the Isle of Wight's coast and the finder returns the island's towns, sorted from the shape's centre — Newport near the middle of the list's geography, the mainland nowhere. Islands are the cleanest demonstration that the polygon, not a radius, is doing the work.

Draw around Cape Cod and the list is the Cape's own towns — Barnstable, Falmouth, out to Provincetown — while a circle of similar size centred mid-Cape would also claim mainland towns across the water. Same centre, different rule, different answer.

popular_table.title: Shape or circle — which finder?
popular_table.intro: Two ways to ask 'what is inside', with different honest uses. This page is the shape column.
popular_table.note: Membership is decided point-in-polygon against the place's recorded point — a town whose point sits just outside your line is out, however much of it spills in.

faq: How is 'inside' decided?
Point-in-polygon: each OpenStreetMap place has a recorded point (its centre node), and the finder tests that point against your drawn shape. The boundary is the whole rule.
Which places count?

Cities and towns as OpenStreetMap records them. Very small settlements may be recorded as villages or hamlets and can fall outside the place classes this finder lists — coverage follows the OSM dataset's richness in that region.
Why did a town I expected not appear?

Three honest causes: its OSM point sits outside your line, it is recorded under a different place class, or the dataset has it under a variant name. Redraw slightly wider and check the map before concluding.
Can the shape have many corners?
Yes — trace coasts and borders with as many clicks as the boundary deserves. More corners, closer fit; the centre and sorting update with the shape.
Is a radius the same as driving distance?
Neither appears here: membership is geometric, not travelled. For road reach from a centre, use the Drive Time Map.
Can I use this for service-area planning?
Yes — it is one of the honest ways to define a service area: draw the real boundary, list the settlements inside, and plan against names rather than impressions.
Are map measurements legal survey measurements?
The polygon is drawn at map accuracy for research and planning. Legal boundaries come from deeds and survey, not from a drawn shape.
Can I draw around a whole county or region?
Yes — bigger shapes are just more corners. Very large polygons return longer lists; the sorting by distance from the centre keeps the heart of the region at the top.
Why is the list sorted from the centre?
Because region questions are usually centre-out: the towns nearest the shape's middle matter first. The Center of Polygon Finder computes that middle explicitly.
Does it include villages?
The finder lists the place classes it is built for — cities and towns in the OpenStreetMap data. A settlement recorded only as a village may not appear; the dataset's local richness decides.
